newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish PM to promote Russia ties despite NATO row.
newsitem.headline: Polish PM to promote Russia ties despite NATO row.

text.p: Poland's Prime Minister visits Russia on Tuesday to underline that the two neighbours can do business, economic and political, despite grave differences over Warsaw's aim to join NATO as fast as it can.

Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz will hold talks with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and other leaders in Moscow, meet officials and businessmen in St Petersburg, then fly to Tatarstan to discuss possible oil imports during the November 12-15 trip.

"The visit underlines our desire to maintain dialogue at the highest level...as often as possible," Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati said last week, recalling that Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski went to Moscow in April.
Polish officials said Cimoszewicz was not expected to meet President Boris Yeltsin, now recovering from heart surgery.
Rosati said the only issue dividing the two countries was the fundamental matter of NATO enlargement.
"I think we have managed to ensure that it should not affect other areas of cooperation...and we want to express this through the visit by Cimoszewicz," he told a news conference.
Russian leaders say NATO's inclusion of Poland, a country of 40 million people bordering its Kaliningrad enclave, will increase a threat to its security from the Western alliance.

Having escaped Soviet domination in 1989, Poland fears Russian pressure on NATO members might dilute the guarantees it seeks as a full member of the pact -- which it expects to join in 1999 as proposed by U.S. President Bill Clinton.
Rosati said he accepted that NATO should reach a strategic agreement with Russia, but wanted this to be done only after Poland was a member and could take part in the negotiations.
Cimoszewicz is likely to focus on economic ties and regulating the legal basis of bilateral relations -- areas where progress is possible.
During the trip the countries are expected at last to sign a long-negotiated settlement of mutual trade debts left from the 1980s, when they were in the now-defunct Comecon bloc.
They are also due to clinch arrangements on air and maritime rescue and on cultural cooperation.
Rosati said, however, that Poland could not now accept proposals by Russian Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Davydov, for a free-trade zone between the two countries.

Russia fears it is losing out as its communist-era trade partners reduce tariffs with each other through the growing Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA) and bind themselves to the European Union they aim to join.
But Rosati said Poland's priority was its agreement with the EU and it could do nothing that might harm progress towards full membership, although it sought easier trade with Russia.
"Russia is neither an EU associate member nor in the World Trade Organisation, so any far-reaching decisions, for instance in opening a free-trade zone, would be...difficult," he said.
The two are not yet near a desired agreement on visa-free travel, because Poland insists on linking this to one obliging Russia to readmit illegal immigrants from third countries.

Rosati said Poland, which has just signed a long-term agreement for natural gas imports from Russia, wanted to import crude oil from the Russian autonomous republic of Tatarstan, which was interested in Polish manufactured goods.
Cimoszewicz, who will be accompanied by a business delegation, will meet Tatarstan political and business leaders in Kazan on November 15 before returning to Warsaw.
